#760. ‘Beds Are Burning,’ ‘Friday on My Mind’ Among First Songs Inducted Into Australia’s National Songbook

An initiative of APRA AMCOS and NFSA, the project preserves "the songs that have helped shape Australia's cultural identity."

Protest, partying, and observations on the great southern land and its people are among the themes that shine through in Australia’s National Songbook, into which the first batch of songs were inducted on Wednesday (Nov. 4). Explore Midnight Oil See latest videos, charts and news

Announced at a special event at the National Film and Sound Archive of Australia in the nation’s capital, Canberra, 10 songs were elevated into The National Songbook, a new, annual initiative that recognizes the songs, songwriters and composers “whose creative vision has given voice to Australian stories.” Related The Lettermen's Tony Butala Dies at 87 Karol G Sweeps Latin Airplay's Top 3 With 'No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto' Tracks Steve Ellis, Love Affair Singer, Dies at 76

Among the standouts, Midnight Oil’s “Beds Are Burning,” the Easybeats’ “Friday on My Mind,” Helen Reddy’s “I Am Woman,” The Presets’ “My People,” Yothu Yindi’s “Treaty,” and Andrew “Banjo” Paterson’s “Waltzing Matilda.”

Reddy’s “I Am Woman,” which topped the Billboard Hot 100 in December 1972, won a Grammy for best pop vocal performance, female, in 1973 and was voted into the U.S.’ National Recording Registry in 2025. The Easybeats’ “Friday on My Mind” and Midnight Oil’s “Beds Are Burning” both reached the top 20 on the Hot 100, in 1967 and 1988, respectively.

An initiative of APRA AMCOS and NFSA, the project preserves “the songs that have helped shape Australia’s cultural identity,” and launches to coincide with APRA’s 100th anniversary.

“No ten songs could ever tell the whole story of Australia, but together these inaugural inductees help us understand, as a nation, where we’ve come from, who we are and the values we’ve carried through generations,” comments Dean Ormston, CEO of APRA AMCOS.

“As APRA celebrates 100 years of championing songwriters, composers and music publishers, we welcome these debut entries into The National Songbook as songs that have helped become part of our shared cultural story, reflecting the extraordinary breadth, diversity and richness of Australian songwriting and composing.”

As it grows, the songbook will serve as a permanent digital archive, a vault that safeguards music treasures for future generations.

“The National Songbook reflects the remarkable breadth of Australian songwriting and composition, from songs of protest, belonging and identity to works that have become woven into our national story and our DNA,” remarks Meagan Loader, chief curator of the NFSA.

“As Australia’s audiovisual archive, the NFSA will ensure these songs and stories are preserved in our national collection of works of significant cultural heritage, heft and heart, providing a new way for Australians now and into the future to engage with the songs and songwriters who have shaped us.”

The inaugural inductees are said to represent more than a century of Australian storytelling, creativity and cultural expression and are selected by an expert panel.

Stream the National Songbook playlists on Apple Music, Spotify and YouTube Music and visit NFSA for more.

Check out the first 10 works entered into The National Songbook:

“Beds Are Burning”Written by Peter Garrett / Rob Hirst / Jim MoginieReleased: 1987

“Down City Streets”Written by Ruby HunterReleased: 1990

“Earth Cry”Composed by Peter SculthorpeReleased: 1990

“Friday on My Mind”Written by Harry Vanda and George YoungReleased: 1966

“I Am Woman”Written by Helen Reddy and Ray BurtonReleased: 1971

“My Island Home”Written by Neil MurrayReleased: 1987 (Warumpi Band) 1995 (Christine Anu)

“My People”Written by Julian Hamilton / Kim MoyesReleased: 2007

The Boys soundtrack by The NecksWritten by Chris Abrahams / Tony Buck / Lloyd SwantonReleased: 1998

“Treaty”Written by Dr M. Yunupingu / Stuart Kellaway / Witiyana Marika / M. Mununggurr / Cal Williams / G. Yunupingu /Peter Garrett / Paul KellyReleased: 1991

“Waltzing Matilda”Written by Andrew ‘Banjo’ Paterson – lyrics, Christina Macpherson – melodyReleased: 1927

Wasn’t it only Florida that was supposed to be this dramatic?

They traded barbs for months and pillaged supporters by the barrel. So it was only fitting after all this that challenger Nithya Raman and incumbent Karen Bass would be deadlocked and separated by just a few thousand votes four hours after the polls closed in the L.A. mayor’s race.Hey, when you’ve got a good show going, you don’t cancel it mid-season.So Raman’s TV writer husband Vali Chandrasekaran could tell you. Or so anyone watching this race could tell you.As of midnight in Los Angeles some 4,000 votes separated Bass, in the lead, with Raman just behind her, with 600,000 votes counted. Given that there are 580,000 votes remaining, that lead tells us nothing.And given the fact that counting takes a long time — anything mail-in ballot postmarked today would still count in the next week — don’t expect a result anytime soon. Related Stories Midterms 2026 Trumper's Remorse: Voters Look at the Last Two Years, Ask for a Redo Midterms 2026 Kimmel Bashes Trump After Democrats' Midterms "Tsunami": "The Only Ass on His Mind Is the One That Just Got Handed to Him"

Raman and Bass are both Democrats, but Raman is to the left of Bass, if not as far to the left as her would-be New York counterpart Zohran Mamdani. #757. BAFTA Breakthrough Ted Evans Shares What Sign Language Taught Him About Film – and What’s Next After ‘Retreat’

The British writer-director, featured on the 2026 U.K. BAFTA Breakthrough list, supported by Netflix, also tells THR how "I always feel I have two audiences" and about his vision for "sign language cinema."

A young woman arrives at a remote wellness retreat for Deaf people, but nothing is what it seems. If you don’t immediately recognize this set-up, you most likely haven’t seen Retreat, the genre-bending debut thriller from British writer-director Ted Evans that has left audiences guessing until the very end.

Billed as “the world’s first deaf thriller” and starring Anne Zander, James Joseph Boyle and Sophie Stone, Retreat, highlighted by THR as a hidden gem, is also a key reason for Evans to feature on the 2026 U.K. BAFTA Breakthrough list of rising talent, supported by Netflix, which was unveiled on Wednesday. Related Stories Movies 'The Incomer' Attracted Domhnall Gleeson and Moby and Got Its Creator on the BAFTA Breakthrough List. Now, He's Working on a Plan B Film. Movies 'Ish' Has Resonated Widely Amid "Authoritarian Turn," Says Its BAFTA Breakthrough Writer-Director

Among his past work, the creative directed the TV documentary Rose Ayling-Ellis: Signs for Change and short films.

THR talked to Evans about making a splash with his first feature, the short he made with the same title, making the BAFTA Breakthrough list, and what’s next.

Sorry to say that my sign language is not up to snuff. How exciting is it to be a BAFTA Breakthrough creative?Oh, it is a huge honor. It was a big surprise just to be acknowledged and to be amongst these amazing creatives, especially my lead actress, Sophie Stone. To be alongside her for this honor is terrific.How similar is the feature Retreat to your short film that had the same title?It’s a long story. So I made a short film of the same name, and it was about a community. But it was a shoestring short I made for hardly any money at all about 14 years ago. That short did well within the community, but I wasn’t satisfied with it – there was so much more.I then spent a decade excavating and developing something, and it became something completely different thematically. It has the same title, and Sophie was in the short as well, but they’re not really connected. The origin story is much more about us as filmmakers and actors coming together, and the project was born out of that.How cool was it to have a film where all the lead cast members are deaf, and I heard behind the scenes there was also a special focus on the community.Yeah, absolutely. As a deaf man, I grew up in this community, and I’m obviously very passionate about what I call “sign language cinema.” We all have stories ourselves. We’re all part of the human experience, and cinema is such a wonderful way to show the full diversity of what it means to be human. To bring deaf people, our languages, and our culture to cinema has been amazing.We had such an amazing cast, and we did have some deaf talent behind the camera as well. We had sign language directors, assistant directors, and runners and stuff like that. So it was great.And as a filmmaker, working with sign language, which is a visual language, taught me so much more about the medium.Can you share some more insight on that?If you think about continuity, you must make sure that with every shot, every take, there is a flow of continuity. And you think about rhythm and visual grammar. Working with sign language has helped me as a filmmaker understand filmmaking.

I’m not saying that spoken language films don’t [focus on the same things], but you can get away with ADR [Automated Dialogue Replacement], replacing dialogue in post. That is completely different when you’re working with sign language.

What are you hoping for from the BAFTA Breakthrough programs?I have lots of ideas. I write, I direct. I’m looking forward to networking to meet people with a lot more experience and connections in the industry, just to work out the next chapter and what’s possible. Obviously, there are lots of pipe dreams, but you’ve got to be realistic in today’s world. Obviously, it’s not easy. I’m just going to be like a sponge, and I’m just excited to learn really and to make more connections.You mentioned you have a lot of ideas. Is there any new film or series that you’re particularly focused on developing?My slate is quite healthy. I’m allowed to say that I have a horror in development with BBC Film, which is in the very, very early stages. I’m really excited about that. I am hoping to work more inside the community as well as hopefully branch outwards. So, it’s an exciting time.Retreat shows different types of sign languages, but the focus is British Sign Language (BSL). Can people from abroad understand that?Really, American Sign Language is very different from British Sign Language, and actually, more countries are influenced by American Sign Language. In Australia, they have Auslan, which is related to BSL, but they’re all languages of their own. But yes, in fact, in Retreat, we have several languages, including German. If you think about Native American tribes in America, they all had their own languages, but they had an actual sign language that was called Hand Talk, and it was a modality for people to trade between different communities.

What’s your hope for Retreat and its impact?Ultimately, I always feel I have two audiences. I have my community, and then I have the rest of the world. For both of them, number one, you want them to go through a thrilling ride. You want them to enjoy the film, but then there are layers that they can go into.

I hope that it’s universal. I hope it’s not just about our experience. It’s about choice. It’s about understanding what makes you who you are, whether it’s your community or the experience you go through, and what happens when you take one of them out. Hopefully it makes people think. We’re releasing the film early next year into cinemas, which I’m really excited about. We’ve had an amazing year starting at Toronto with our world premiere, and we traveled around the world a lot. So, I just feel really blessed and honored.

#756. Ozzfest 2027 Begins Countdown to … Something

The returning metal fest appears to be gearing up for a major announcement this week.

Fans jacked about the return of Ozzfest may finally have some answers about what the rebooted metal festival will look like on Thursday (Nov. 5). That’s because the hard rock touring event launched by late metal icon Ozzy Osbourne in 1996 started a countdown clock on Tuesday morning that is set to expire at 10 a.m. ET on Thursday morning alongside the caption, “Countdown’s begun.”

At press time no additional information was available on what Thursday’s revelation will be, but Ozzfest has been teasing out the news for the past week, including with a cryptic post featuring the caption “Tell me people…” alongside the iconic O from the Ozzfest logo bisecting a devil’s head. Even more enigmatic was a post over the weekend featuring a sea of white question marks on a black screen.

Ozzy’s widow and longtime manager, Sharon Osbourne, told Billboard earlier this year that she’d been in talks with Live Nation about bringing the festival back next year. “It was something Ozzy was very passionate about: giving young talent a stage in front of a lot of people,” she said. “We really started metal festivals in this country. It was [replicated but] never done with the spirit of what ours was, because ours was a place for new talent. It was like summer camp for kids.” The news was followed a few weeks later by an Ozzfest post that read “Ozzfest could return — 2027?”

The dream then became a reality, with Ozzfest confirming that its reboot will include a stop a Villa Park in Osbourne’s hometown of Birmingham, U.K. next year, as well as the first U.S. dates in nearly a decade. In an Instagram post on Sept. 21, the event announced, “Ozzfest will come to the U.K. and U.S. @theozzfest,” with the caption promising, “More Info Coming Soon!!! Where are you hoping Ozzfest 2027 will pop up?”

And while info is scarce at this moment, fans had plenty of ideas in the countdown post comments, including: “Remaining members of Black Sabbath with Zakk Wylde as lead singer. Black label society opens up!,” “Here we go 🤘 can’t wait to see who’s playing,” “Lineup announcement imminent?,” “Slayer Slayer Slayer” and “Youg Blood headlining.”

Ozzfest was launched by Sharon Osbourne in 1996 after she was unable to book Ozzy on the Lollapalooza festival. Ozzfest then quickly became a popular annual touring festival that brought a day of hard rock and heavy metal to the U.S. and Europe through 2008. Since then, it has taken place on a more sporadic schedule, most recently as a one-day event in 2018 at The Forum in Inglewood, California, with a lineup that featured Rob Zombie, Body Count, Marilyn Manson and others.

#754. ‘Ulya’ Director Dives Into His Third Latvian Oscar Contender, Which Stars a Rising Actor as a Female Basketball Legend and Became a “Blockbuster”

Viesturs Kairišs also shares Herzog and Bergman inspirations for the film, opening Tallinn and starring Kārlis Arnolds Avots as Uljana Semjonova, the first non-U.S. woman in the Basketball Hall of Fame.

Latvia made Oscar history in 2025 when Gints Zilbalodis‘ Flow won the best animated feature award. Two years later, the country has selected a very different movie to represent it at the Oscars 2027. The Baltic country picked Ulya from director Viesturs Kairišs (January), which stars up-and-coming Latvian actor Kārlis Arnolds Avots and world-premiered at Cannes in the Un Certain Regard section, as its international best feature film Oscar contender.

Inspired by the life of legendary Latvian basketball player Uljana Semjonova, a two-time Olympic champion and three-time world champion, the black-and-white Ulya follows its protagonist from an isolated rural Old Believer community into the fiercely competitive world of professional basketball. There, she must navigate both the attention drawn by her extraordinary height and the demands of elite sport. Related Stories Movies BAFTA Breakthrough Ted Evans Shares What Sign Language Taught Him About Film - and What's Next After 'Retreat' Movies 'The Incomer' Attracted Domhnall Gleeson and Moby and Got Its Creator on the BAFTA Breakthrough List. Now, He's Working on a Plan B Film.

Semjonova ended up winning the Soviet Union’s national championship and the European Champions Cup 15 times each, the Olympic Gold medal with the USSR in 1976 and 1980, and she became the first non-U.S. woman in the Basketball Hall of Fame.

On Friday, Ulya will open the 30th edition of Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF). As a co-production between Latvia, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania, it is also a symbol for the rise of Baltic cinema on the world stage. “Ulya is a very good example of what the Baltic film industries can achieve by working together and with partners beyond our region,” said Triin Tramberg, artistic director of PÖFF. “Our countries may be small, but we have a wealth of stories and creative talent. Co-productions bring those strengths together, help ambitious films reach audiences around the world and give our filmmakers a stronger international presence.”

Avots wrote the script with Livia Ulman and Andris Feldmanis. Wojciech Staroń is the cinematographer, with editing by Armands Zacs. B-Rated International is handling sales for Ulya, produced by Ego Media in Latvia, Allfilm in Estonia, Staroń Film in Poland and Tremora in Lithunia. New Mountain Films has acquired Ulya for North America.

Latvia, which has a population of about 1.8 million, comparable to that of West Virginia, has previously sent two other Kairišs films to the Oscars: his 2022 movie January, a coming-of-age story about an aspiring filmmaker looking to find himself against the backdrop of Latvian independence, and his 2017 film The Chronicles of Melanie, based on the real-life story of a woman who, along with her son, was sent to a labor camp in Siberia in the 1940s after the Soviet occupation of Latvia.

Kairišs talked to THR about Ulya, bringing to life the inner world of a legendary athlete, and how the film, has become a blockbuster in Latvia.

The filmmaker and Avots previously worked together on January. And Kairišs knew that the star was considering writing a play about Semjonova and starring in it. “I heard from Kārlis for a while that his dream was to play Uljana Semjonova,” the director tells THR. When the star told another creative about the idea, “I realized, wow, it’s a film. It’s not a theater play.”

Kairišs didn’t have his eyes on a historical project. “I was a little bit tired of making films connected with Latvian history,” he recalls. “I was not very interested in making something about sports or whatever. But I heard the story about a giant girl living in the deep countryside and then coming to Riga, with the coaches of that time taking her away. And I was seriously touched by this beginning. I immediately had this first image in my head about some far-away environment where a strange tall girl lives, and people suddenly start to look for her.”

Having a male play the female basketball legend was not something he dwelt on. “This was a package. Kārlis is playing Ulya,” Kairišs says. “For me, it was immediately okay. I had to do it. But when we were looking for co-producers’ money, very often people were concerned about how it would look and if it would [seem like] a caricature or something. But I always said it sounds great. It’s a film about Ulya, and it’s not my idea. And I’m totally not interested in just a, let’s say, ‘normal’ or traditional film.”

Avots told THR earlier this year that, for him, Ulya felt like a story similar to Werner Herzog’s The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser. And his director had the same instinct. “My first impulse was that this is a little bit like a Werner Herzog film about a giant,” he shares.

Asked about other influences, the director mentions that he suggested that he and cinematographer Staroń watch Ingmar Bergman’s psychological drama Persona. “It’s probably an influence, or an influence on the aesthetic,” Kairišs acknowledges.

But the physical look and movements were mainly key to diving inside the person at the heart of the film. “My first major task for myself and the artistic team was how to go into her mind,” the filmmaker tells THR. “I was interested in showing the film from her inside right from the beginning. Of course, there are a lot of objective things, but I still found it important to show the invisible world of this human.”

As Avots told THR earlier in the year, Semjonova was a neighbor of his in Latvia’s capital, Riga. They developed a bond, and she trusted the team behind the film. The end of Ulya features a symbol of that bond: a photo of the athlete, who died in January, with Avots.

Focusing on one special person and her challenges and story helped make the film feel universal, the filmmaker believes. “While we were trying to go inside her head and make a very subjective film, it somehow also became a film about all of us – everybody who can identify with having an inner freak that we hold inside,” Kairišs offers. “Everybody has something that you want to hide that responds to all the standards that the modern world demands of you. You are somehow killing your darling, probably, your real authenticity, so the film is very universal.”

How does the director feel about Ulya representing Latvia in the international Oscar race? “It’s my third time,” he emphasizes. “You go to those Oscars with a small budget from Latvia, but the response to the film at screenings has always been amazing. And [premiering at] the Cannes festival was a dream for me.”

Kairišs also emphasizes the box-office success that Ulya has become back home. “In Latvia, it’s a real blockbuster,” reaching around 105,000 admissions and counting since its launch earlier this year, he says. That makes Ulya the most successful Latvian film in the country’s cinemas in 2026, putting it ahead of such Hollywood blockbusters as The Odyssey and Minions & Monsters. It is currently even the second most successful film of 2026 overall in Latvian cinemas, just behind Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Says its director: “It’s an unbelievable success for a black-and-white art house film.”

#753. Ukraine tries to shut Moscow's airports with drone strikes on Russia

Repeated Ukrainian drone attacks are increasingly disrupting operations at Moscow's airports. The pounding is part of Ukraine's plan to shut down Russia's airpace.

For months, drone strikes by Ukraine have forced the suspension of flights to and from airports in Russia. Moscow's Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Zhukovsky and Vnukovo airports have had to shut down operations almost daily in October, according to reports from the independent investigative media outlet Agentstvo. On some days, the airports were reportedly closed for up to nine hours.

In early September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine would seek to cut off the airspace around Moscow and other destinations in Russia. "Today, we would like to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who continues to use major Russian airports: Russian airspace will become completely unsafe," Zelenskyy said.

The following day, Ukraine sent a corresponding warning to the International Civil Aviation Organization.

Ukraine's airspace has been closed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia's aviation authority, Rosaviatsiya, has issued an emergency safety "carpet" protocol that is designed to immediately shut down the airspace over a specific region or around affected airports if an aircraft violates Russian airspace, weapons are used, or unidentified objects appear in the skies. Once the protocol is announced, drastic restrictions apply to all air traffic.

"If there is a military threat, a specific section of airspace is closed off, and this carpet is declared," Oleksandr Laneckij, the chief executive officer of the Friendly Avia Support consultancy, told DW. "Essentially, every drone poses a military threat."

Laneckij noted that Yemen's Houthis have managed to significantly disrupt Saudi airspace. "I think Ukraine's military capabilities far exceed those of the Houthis," Laneckij said.

The military analyst Jan Matvejev also said Ukraine would have little trouble severely disrupting Moscow-area air traffic. Though Ukraine has not yet managed to completely shut down Russian airspace as Zelenskyy plans, Matvejev said, its armed forces "remain committed to this idea."

"To close off the airspace and trigger the 'carpet' plan, all you need are simple drones that don't have to be equipped with a warhead or even have a long range," Matvejev said. Ukraine's arms industry can produce hundreds of combat-ready long-range drones in a day, he added. That is why he believes Ukraine could have the necessary resources to shut down Moscow's airports.

Indeed, Ukraine's efforts to shut down Russian airspace are "just getting started," Simon Shuster wrote in October in the US magazine The Atlantic, citing well-informed sources.

Matvejev said Russia's air-defense systems were not entirely effective in efforts to prevent Ukrainian drones from penetrating Moscow's airspace. "If it were possible to shoot them down, they would have done so by now," he said. He added that Russia would have deployed additional air-defense troops if they were available.

Laneckij said Russia might lower the threshold for declaring the carpet protocol, which could increase the risk of deadly incidents such as the 2024 Christmas day crash of an Azerbaijan Airlines flight. Investigators say the flight was struck by a Russian air-defense missile that was being used to defend against drones, killing 38 people.

Matvejev seconded the fear that Russia's defenses could again mistakenly target civilian aircraft instead of military objects. He said little had changed about Russia's air-defense protocol since the Azeri flight was shot in 2024.

In an operation against a low-flying drone, the target is visually identified and fired upon with a machine gun. In such a scenario, the danger to aircraft is extremely low, unless they happen to be flying in the immediate vicinity.

The risk to civil aviation increases significantly when anti-aircraft missiles are deployed, Matvejev said. A missile could have defects that are practically unavoidable in mass production and could veer toward an aircraft flying nearby. Matvejev said such defense measures could not guarantee the safety of civilian aircraft during operations.

He said drones did not have to carry explosives to be disruptive. A collision between an airplane and a basic drone can have serious consequences — and, he said, a drone sent from Ukraine all the way to Moscow must be relatively large, "weighting dozens of kilograms."

In the summer of 2023, Ukrainian armed forces attacked the airport in the Russian city of Pskov, where both military and civilian aircraft were parked. Earlier this month, drone debris fell on the Sochi airport, on Russia's Black Sea coast.

Russia also attacks Ukraine's airports. In September, Zelenskyy said Kyiv's airport had been struck, as well as the Boryspil airport near the capital.

Laneckij said three factors would determine whether international airlines suspend their flights to Russia: the military threat, the degree of demand and the insurance cost.

He said issues could emerge around insurance. When insurers rate the security risk of flying to Russia as very high, they could significantly raise their rates for aircraft headed there. This would cause ticket prices to skyrocket.

Competition within Russia's aviation market has already declined because many airlines are no longer in business, Laneckij said. This has increased demand for tickets from the remaining foreign airlines.

"Whether they stay or not depends on the price they have to pay for the danger faced," he said.

#752. Brandi Carlile, Leon Thomas & Magnus Ferrell Christmas Covers (Plus a JYT Original) Adorn Starbucks’ First Holiday Album in More Than a Decade

Coco Jones, TRÍADA & The Womack Sisters are also featured on Holiday Blend, which arrives today on streaming services & coffeehouse playlists.

For the first time in more than a decade, Starbucks is getting back into the holiday music business.

The new album Holiday Blend — featuring Christmas covers from Brandi Carlile, Leon Thomas, Coco Jones, Magnus Ferrell, TRÍADA and The Womack Sisters and a yuletide original from the boy band JYT — arrives Wednesday (Nov. 4) on streaming services and coffeehouse playlists via Interscope Records and Universal Music Group, Billboard can exclusively reveal.

The last time Starbucks put out a holiday album was Holidays Rule back in 2012, which featured The Shins, Fun., The Civil Wars, Paul McCartney and more.

For the new album, Carlile performs Joni Mitchell’s “River,” which starts with the holiday-set lyrics “It’s coming on Christmas/ They’re cutting down trees/ They’re putting up reindeer/ And singing songs of joy and peace.” Thomas gets us ready for a funky, festive holiday with his version of James Brown’s “Soulful Christmas.”

Ferrell — who covers the “Happy Holiday / The Holiday Season” medley released by Andy Williams in 1963 — says being part of Holiday Blend “felt like a chance to make something that’s both new and nostalgic. I grew up hearing these songs, so getting to record them in my own way was a pretty special experience.”

For her take on “It’s the Most Wonderful Time of the Year” — another 1963 Williams release — Jones said she “was honored and excited to put my own spin on such a beloved holiday classic, and I hope my version brings a little extra joy to people’s celebrations this season.”

The boy band JYT contributes the brand-new song “This Christmas” to Holiday Blend, and the quintet is “pumped” to be part of the Starbucks compilation. “The idea that someone could be ordering a Refresher and hear our song playing is actually crazy,” reads a statement from the group. (Sample lyric: “It’s just you on my wish list/ All I need is your peppermint kisses.”) “This Christmas” was written and produced by JYT mastermind Freddy Wexler, along with co-writer Elliah Heifetz and co-producer Gian Stone.

TRÍADA contribute the only Spanish-language song on the album, with their cover of Luis Miguel’s “Llegó La Navidad,” which itself is a spin on “Winter Wonderland.” “We hope this version feels familiar and fresh at the same time,” the Argentine trio says. “The song has such a beautiful feeling at its heart, and singing it in Spanish let us connect with it in our own way.”

Finally, The Womack Sisters serve up a Stevie Wonder classic, covering his 1967 hit “What Christmas Means to Me.” “For our family, Christmas is the best time of the year,” the R&B trio says. “The holidays are about togetherness, so singing ‘What Christmas Means to Me’ felt like a natural way to celebrate the season and share a piece of that family connection.”

Holiday Blend will also honor the season of giving by including a $500,000 donation to World Central Kitchen to support humanitarian relief efforts around the world.

“Music has always been part of the Starbucks experience, and we are building on that legacy in a way that feels fresh for today,” says Erin Silvoy, Starbucks’ senior vice president, global marketing & channel development. “Holiday Blend brings together incredible artists to put their own spin on songs we all know and love. My hope is that it becomes part of the soundtrack to the season, creating a little more joy and connection whether you’re in a Starbucks coffeehouse or wherever the holidays take you.”

Starbucks has a long history in music, starting with the acquisition of music retailer Hear Music in 1999 and continuing with exclusive music releases in partnership with Concord Music Group. Back in 2006, a Billboard article reported annual album sales of 3.6 million units or approximately $65 million in music revenue via Starbucks. In 2015, Starbucks coffee shops stopped selling CDs, but the brand has continued its music efforts, including a longstanding partnership with Spotify.

#751. Democrats Just Took the House and the Senate. Get Ready for a Whole Lot of Media Investigations.

David Ellison, Lachlan Murdoch, Mark Zuckerberg and other moguls are likely to find themselves facing inquiries, and perhaps hearings, over their deals and Trump ties.

In early February, just a few weeks before David Ellison’s Paramount secured its deal to pry Warner Bros. Dicovery from Netflix’s grasp, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos and WBD chief revenue and strategy officer Bruce Campbell were hauled before Congress to defend their deal.

“I want to thank Mr. Sarandos and Mr. Campbell for coming here,” Sen. Cory Booker said in his opening remarks. “It is not fun often to testify before Congress. Sometimes I wonder if it ranks higher than a visit to the proctologist or to the dentist.”

What followed were tough, pointed, and sometimes overtly political questions, which Sarandos and Campbell had to navigate. Sen. Hawley, for example, accused Netflix of hosting content that “promotes a transgender ideology.”

Ellison had been invited, but declined, citing the fact that, after all, Paramount’s bid had been rejected by WBD.

The next Congress is unlikely to accept that answer.

Nor can he just ignore Congressional Democrats’ inquiries into his dealings, as he did last year.

With Democrats securing the House and the Senate in stunning fashion, the investigations into the Trump administration on Capitol Hill will begin. And there is reason to believe that the administration’s relationship with media companies, both positive and negative, will be among their top priorities. And yes, subpoenas may be in order.

Congress may not be able to block any deals they don’t like, but they can inflict pain through investigations and forced disclosures. And attention all CEOs: If Democrats in power get their wish, you should be prepared to testify.

A source working for one Democratic senator says that members of Congress in both houses are eager to haul executives in to ask about their deals and any rumored quid pro quos, with Skydance’s mega-deal for WBD and the ongoing Fox-Roku deal drawing particular scrutiny, as is the TikTok U.S. sale to Oracle, Silver Lake, and MGX.

Also of interest are the deals big tech companies like Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX have with the government for data centers, AI, and other services, and, yes, perhaps Amazon’s deal for the Melania Trump documentary, which its chairman Jeff Bezos framed as a “very wise business decision.”

Skydance’s move to raise cash from Middle East sovereign wealth funds and others like SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk is also of interest.

Booker made his intentions clear in a statement after Paramount’s settlement with the state AGs:

“This merger is the product of corruption hiding in plain sight. Secretary Hegseth stood in the Pentagon press room and said he couldn’t wait for the Ellisons to take over. Paramount was a constant presence at the Justice Department once it needed the deal pushed through. But when Congress asked questions, the company ignored our inquiries and refused invitations to testify. On the night of the shareholder vote, Ellison hosted a dinner honoring President Trump. Then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, the official responsible for approving this deal, was in attendance,” Booker wrote.

“This administration has turned merger review into a marketplace for political favors,” he continued. “That is why I will examine every merger this administration has approved, and why I will keep fighting to pass the CLEAN Mergers Act, so that no company can ever again buy its way past the law.”

At the same time, there is a desire to investigate what they see as overreach by the administration, particularly as it relates to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, which is in the process of attempting to strip Disney’s ABC of its local TV station licenses, and may be in a position to review NBC’s licenses shortly pending the NBCUniversal spinoff from Comcast. Anthropic’s feud with the DOJ may also come under scrutiny.

Any one of those deals could see the media companies brought before Congress to address their treatment by the administration, but also expose them to online attacks and revelatory details that they may prefer to avoid.

Just look at the child safety hearings held by Congress in 2024, where tech executives like Mark Zuckerberg, Evan Spiegel, Shou Xhew and Linda Yaccarino were put through the ringer (Zuckerberg memorably was asked to turn and apologize to families of victims of abuse).

The window for dealmakers to get major media, entertainment or tech deals through D.C. without that proverbial proctology exam may be nearing an end.

#750. Coca-Cola hikes earnings outlook, even as it sees lackluster demand in North America

Coca-Cola on Tuesday raised its full-year outlook for the third straight quarter, despite lackluster demand in its home market.

For the full year, Coke now expects comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from its prior forecast of an increase in the range of 9% to 10%. The beverage giant also anticipates that its organic revenue will climb at least 5%, a slight increase from its previous outlook of approximately 5% growth.

CEO Henrique Braun attributed the company's strong results to its "speed and discipline" despite the "uneven environment," he said on the company's earnings conference call.

Looking ahead to 2027, the company expects consumer behavior to remain unchanged, CFO John Murphy said. In recent quarters, Braun and other executives have said North American shoppers are under pressure, stretched thin by inflation and economic uncertainty, and looking for value. But the beverage giant has also said consumers are still buying its drinks, from premium brands like Fairlife to its namesake soda.

Shares of the company fell less than 1% in morning trading on its gloomy forecast for the consumer environment.

Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street analysts surveyed by LSEG were expecting:

Coke reported fiscal third-quarter net income attributable to shareholders of $4.01 billion, or 93 cents per share, up from $3.7 billion, or 86 cents per share, a year earlier.

Excluding transaction gains and other items, Coke earned 91 cents per share.

Net sales rose 7% to $13.4 billion. Coke's organic revenue, which strips out acquisitions, divestitures and foreign currency, also climbed 7% in the quarter.

For the second straight quarter, the company's unit case volume increased 5%, helped by higher demand outside of North America.

Coke's home market reported flat volume. However, the company's North American business would have reported volume growth if not for the timing of the Fourth of July holiday and the monthslong shortage of Topo Chico, a sparkling water brand Coke owns, Murphy told CNBC.

"The underlying momentum remains quite strong," he said. "Consumer sentiment is largely unchanged in the sense that, wherever you are on the income scale, you're looking for value, and I think our system here has done a good job interpreting that."

In North America, Coke's at-home business is faring better than its away-from-home segment, which includes restaurants, movie theaters and amusement parks. The restaurant industry is still under pressure, and Coke expects that to continue through the rest of the year, Murphy told analysts on the company's earnings conference call.

Globally, Coke's sparkling soft drinks business saw volume increase 5% during the quarter, lifted by growth of Coke, Coke Zero Sugar and Diet Coke.

Diet Coke is having a "resurgence," Murphy told CNBC. Gen Z consumers in the U.S. have nicknamed it a "fridge cigarette," while consumers in India threw Diet Coke parties as shortages tied to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran have made the drink scarce.

"It's a brand that's almost reinventing itself with the next generation of consumers," he said.

Coke has also gained market share as rival PepsiCo sees its soda business struggle, according to Murphy. Still, some of Coke's soda brands, like Sprite, have "some work to do."

Coke's water, sports, coffee and tea division also saw volume climb by 5%. Increased demand for its water, which includes its premium Smartwater brand, fueled the growth. Demand for its tea and coffee was flat, while sports drinks declined.

The company's juice, value-added dairy and plant-based beverages business reported flat volume, despite growth in brands like Fairlife and Minute Maid.

#749. Hailey Bieber Details Emotional Rollercoaster of PMDD Diagnosis After Son Jack Blues’ Birth: ‘Just a Really Intense and Special Journey’

The model and Rhode founder has talked before about the difficulty of premenstrual dysphoric disorder, a more severe form of premenstrual syndrome.

Hailey Bieber has been an open book when it comes to the joy of motherhood, but she has also been very frank about some of the challenges of raising son Jack Blues with husband Justin Bieber. In a new interview with Women’s Wear Daily, the 29-year-old model and founder of Rhode cosmetics talked about her struggle with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a severe, hormonally driven mood disorder that is a more intense form of premenstrual syndrome. Related 23 Best Christmas Gifts for Teens, From TikTok-Approved Finds to Pop Culture Favorites Watch Ariana Grande Crash an Interview With Her 'Focker-in-Law' Castmates The Criterion Collection Unveils 'KPop Demon Hunters' Edition: Here's Where to Shop the 4K Blu-ray & DVD Online Explore Hailey Bieber See latest videos, charts and news

“After I had my son, I struggled with [PMDD] a bit, and there’s just not a lot of conversation or research around it,” said Bieber.

According to Johns Hopkins Medicine, PMDD is a severe and chronic health condition whose symptoms start the week before menstruation and can include depressed mood and feelings of hopelessness, increased anxiety, mood swings, self-critical thoughts, sudden tearfulness, increased irritability and concentration problems, among others.

Bieber said that during her pregnancy and after Jack Blues’ birth she experienced very intense emotional symptoms that made her realize that there is not enough conversation or research about a number of health issues women face.

“Especially after having my own child. That was just a really intense and special journey that I had,” she said. “There’s so much that happens when you are pregnant, during childbirth. There’s so many things that happen leading up to having a child.” Bieber said she kept having PMDD symptoms postpartum and after Jack’s birth, “I struggled with that a bit, and there’s just not a lot of conversation or research around it.”

Bieber, who has spoken about her PMDD struggles before, said speaking in public about it makes her feel “less alone,” and she hopes that it might lead to more open conversations among women in order to make it feel like “less of a lonely journey” for others. As a result of her experience, Rhode recently announced a $5 million, three-year partnership with the Foundation for Women’s Health to support medical research, education and care in areas typically underfunded.

Hailey and Justin welcomed Jack in August 2024 and back in March she first opened up about her PMDD diagnosis on the SHE MD podcast, where she said she’d been diagnosed with the disorder six months after giving birth.

“I was like, ‘This just feels way more intense than before,’ like the lead-up to getting your period,” she said in the previous interview of the emotional tumult she felt after Jack’s birth, which she described as much different from the PMS she’d experienced before. “You’re like, ‘Why does it feel like my whole entire life is gonna end? Like, I don’t understand.’ You just have all these swirling thoughts and feelings, and just everything feels like the biggest deal in the world.”

Bieber also explained that once her period began some of those more intense feelings began to recede and improve with time. In 2022, Beiber was hospitalized for a ministroke and then subsequently had a successful procedure to close a small hole in her heart.

#748. Trans Rights Protesters Crash Grand Opening of U.K.’s Largest ‘Harry Potter’ Store

Author J.K. Rowling has long been criticized for her transphobia, with the controversy only getting louder as the release of HBO's TV show adaptation nears.

The grand opening of a flagship Harry Potter store on London’s Oxford Street has been disrupted by transgender rights protesters.

A group gathered outside the building — officially the U.K.’s largest Harry Potter shop, spanning 21,000 square feet and two floors at The Ribbon development — on Wednesday with signs reading “protect trans lives” and “stop funding trans erasure.” According to U.K. outlet The Standard, they led chants through a megaphone and told those entering the enormous store: “You should not be reading Harry Potter to your children and then bringing them to this store.” Related Stories Oscars 2027: Int'l Films in Focus 'Ulya' Director Dives Into His Third Latvian Oscar Contender, Which Stars a Rising Actor as a Female Basketball Legend and Became a "Blockbuster" Movies BAFTA Breakthrough Ted Evans Shares What Sign Language Taught Him About Film - and What's Next After 'Retreat'

The protesters also drew the trans flag and statements such as “Buy another author” and “Harry Potter isn’t the only kids’ book” in chalk on the sidewalk outside. Police were also called and stationed outside.

Among the film stars celebrating the store’s opening were Draco Malfoy actor Tom Felton and Warwick Davis, who is set to reprise his role as Professor Filius Flitwick in the upcoming TV show adaptation of Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone on HBO.

Franchise author J.K. Rowling, a staunch advocate for anti-trans policies in Britain, has regularly come under fire for her transphobia. She has often been publicly criticized over her politics and creation of The J.K. Rowling Women’s Fund, a legal fund for individuals pushing anti-transgender views across the country.

The controversy has been renewed by the TV series, with stars John Lithgow (playing Albus Dumbledore), Nick Frost (Rubeus Hagrid) and Bel Powley (Petunia Dursley) among the cast members distancing themselves from Rowling’s views. She serves as an executive producer on the series.

“I find it ironic and somewhat inexplicable that Rowling has expressed such views,” said Lithgow earlier this year. “I’ve read about them, and I’ve never met her. She’s not really involved in this production at all. The people who are re-adapting Harry Potter and turning it into an eight-year-long TV series are remarkable. … These are people I really want to work with.”

Powley said in August: “I strongly disagree with J.K. Rowling’s views on gender. I think that the trans community deserve safety and dignity and respect and total acceptance,” while Frost said last year: “[Rowling]’s allowed her opinion and I’m allowed mine, they just don’t align in any way, shape or form.”

The protest comes just days before the ceremonial unveiling of Oxford Street’s Harry Potter Christmas lights, timed to coincide with the launch of the TV series, and which have been promised to transform the city’s most iconic shopping destination into “one of the world’s most beloved stories, bringing a host of Potter-inspired celebrations and attractions to shoppers, commuters, international visitors and fans throughout the festive season.”

More than 11,000 people have signed a petition calling for London mayor Sadiq Khan to “pull the plug on transphobia” and axe the Potter-themed display. “Sadiq Khan says he’s an ally of the trans community, declaring that trans rights are human rights, and that London will remain a safe, welcoming space for trans people,” wrote organizers the Good Law Project. “So why is he allowing one of the most famous anti-trans people in the world to take over Oxford Street?”

The Hollywood Reporter has approached reps for J.K. Rowling and the store for comment.

#747. Boeing says it won't significantly ramp up 737 Max production until late 2027

Boeing doesn't expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027 as it grapples with a slower-than-expected pace of wing production.

CEO Kelly Ortberg said Tuesday on the company's quarterly earnings call that Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.

Ortberg had told investors last month that the production stabilize was taking a "little bit longer" than expected because of the wings production pace.

Boeing stock fell 10% in trading Tuesday.

"I know everybody wants us to go faster, but we're going to do it right," Ortberg told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview Tuesday.

Ortberg reiterated the company's priority in stabilizing production on Tuesday.

"Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality."

Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it.

The company also reported Tuesday that it narrowed its losses in the third quarter, thanks to a boost from its defense unit.

For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company posted a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program.

Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025.

The company's defense unit revenue jumped 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion.

Here's what Boeing reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:

Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier.

Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said.

Ortberg told staff in a memo that the manufacturer has "more work to do."

The manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet.

And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10, the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the 737 Max 7 in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line.

#746. Sky’s $2.1 Billion ITV Megadeal: U.K. Regulators Get Gov’t Green Light for Investigation

Culture secretary Lisa Nandy had previously said she was "minded to intervene," citing “public interest considerations.”

Now it is official. The U.K. government has filed an intervention notice into the planned $2.1 billion takeover of ITV’s TV networks and streaming assets by Comcast‘s Sky, U.K. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said on Wednesday. That means she is asking regulators Ofcom and the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to formally investigate the deal.

While Ofcom’s review will focus on the proposed merger’s public interest impact, the CMA will review it from a competition perspective.

The ITV-Sky deal promises to bring together Britain’s largest pay-TV operator with its largest commercial free-to-air broadcaster. Sky CEO Dana Strong called it “a defining moment for British media.” ITV CEO Carolyn McCall touted it as the creation of “a U.K. champion with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms.” But critics have expressed concerns about the merged entity’s market power. On Wednesday, Nandy shared that the companies had submitted their reactions to the expressed concerns. “Having fully considered their representations, I have decided to issue a Public Interest Intervention Notice,” a so-called PIIN, Nandy said in parliament.

In a statement, Nandy’s office outlined several key reasons for a public interest deal review, including “the need for free expression of opinion in news media,” the goal of “a sufficient plurality of views in news media in each market for news media in the United Kingdom or a part of the United Kingdom,” and “the need for the availability throughout the United Kingdom of a wide range of broadcasting and on-demand programs.”

ITV agreed to sell its media and entertainment arm to Sky for £1.6 billion in July. The deal covers ITV’s terrestrial TV channels and streaming service ITVX. Production arm ITV Studios would continue operating as a separate company.

Sky is led by CEO Dana Strong. It not only operates pay-TV and streaming businesses in the U.K., Ireland and Italy but also has been growing its telecom offerings, such as broadband and mobile phone operations. Sky also owns the production arm Sky Studios, which is led by Cécile Frot-Coutaz and has been growing its investment in original content creation. Recent Sky Studios productions have included the likes of Mary & George, starring Julianne Moore; The Tattooist of Auschwitz, starring Harvey Keitel; and The Day of the Jackal, starring Eddie Redmayne. Comcast acquired Sky in 2018.

#745. Hollywood Sat Out the Billionaire-Tax Fight. Its Workers Could Pay the Price.

The tax, which appears headed for defeat, would have expanded coverage for the industry's workforce as union members struggle to reach annual minimums.

California’s proposed billionaire tax is heading toward defeat, striking a blow to the struggling Hollywood workers who stood to gain healthcare coverage from the measure and delivering a victory to its super-rich opponents.

With about half the votes counted early Wednesday morning, the “no” vote held a commanding lead of nearly 13 points, or one million votes, making passage very unlikely.

The ballot-measure fight was one of the costliest in state history. More than $350 million was poured into the billionaire tax battle, with opponents and allied campaigns accounting for over 96 percent of that figure.

The national conversation on the initiative has transformed it into a referendum on the power controlled by a handful of the nation’s richest people, like Sergey Brin and Peter Thiel, who spent big bucks opposing the proposal. Hollywood largely stayed out of the fight despite what appears to be an increasingly urgent situation emerging in which workers across the industry are failing to qualify for union health insurance plans.

“It’s hard out there right now,” says Cheyenne Jackson, known for his onscreen roles in several seasons of American Horror Story, 30 Rock and Glee. Last month, he launched One Job Away, a project meant to highlight actors in need of a few more gigs to meet the SAG-AFTRA annual minimum to get health insurance. He says he’s already received hundreds of inquiries from union members at risk of losing coverage.

Under the initiative, a one-time five percent tax would’ve been imposed on the state’s 200-ish billionaires with net worths above $1 billion. It’s aimed at shoring up the state’s healthcare fund to offset federal cuts. That includes Medi-Cal and other coverage programs for low-income Californians, potentially providing a backstop for entertainment workers who lose employer- or union-sponsored insurance. Other possible beneficiaries of the tax: freelancers and other low-income workers, like grips, set decorators, costume designers, editors and production assistants, among others in the entertainment workforce who mostly get seasonal work. The measure could’ve helped preserve or expand the safety net for a large swath of Hollywood behind the camera.

In recent years, actors have struggled to qualify for health insurance because of the sharp drop-off of scripted television series orders and productions opting to shoot in other countries amid industry cost-cutting. Actors on the SAG-AFTRA plan are increasingly having a tough time meeting quarterly deadlines to qualify by reaching $28,000 in earnings.

In total, roughly 22% of workers in the arts, entertainment, recreation and accommodation industry were enrolled in Medi-Cal in 2023, according to a survey from the UC Berkeley Labor Center. The Motion Picture Television Fund has increasingly been providing financial assistance and services to industry members. In 2024, it helped more than 1,100 low-income or uninsured workers obtain health care coverage, including Medi-Cal and Covered California plans.

“Everybody was silent on this,” says Ashley Craig, a volunteer for Patriotic Millionaires, a group that includes Disney scion Tim Disney among the ranks that supports the tax.

“That’s the billion-dollar question,” Jackson says of Hollywood’s collective silence. “Some conversations need to happen.”

For a workforce grappling with a growing health insurance gap, the prospect of new funding should’ve been appealing. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, however, emerged as one of the biggest opponents of the measure, arguing that the tax would drive California’s wealthiest residents and their businesses out of the state. Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg threatened to leave if the measure passed.

Earlier this year, Steven Spielberg moved from California to New York, stirring speculation that he was trying to dodge the tax. He’s one of the few in Hollywood who could’ve been assessed the 5% levy since the measure takes into account intellectual property rights among the assets subject to valuation, and Spielberg has a cache of them. Other potential Hollywood payees include George Lucas, David Geffen and Oprah Winfrey.

The political dynamics surrounding the tax laid bare Newsom’s recent intervention in California’s lawsuit to block Paramount’s $110 billion bid to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery. He played the role of unofficial mediator, inserting himself into negotiations to encourage a settlement. “I’m very mindful of what this means to the state — our reputation,” he said at a press appearance in August, adding that he took CEO David Ellison’s threat to move out of California “seriously.”

The episode offered a window into the political leverage Ellison exercised for government approval of the takeover. Newsom’s opposition to Prop. 40 — and his endorsement of Prop. 42, a billionaire-backed measure headed for victory that would effectively prohibit many future wealth taxes — underscored his alignment with powerful figures who’ve been increasingly emboldened to exercise political clout.

“Newsom really set the tone,” Craig says.

#744. Scientists discover a hidden oxygen reservoir deep inside Earth

Scientists have discovered that molten rock deep inside Earth can store far more oxygen than previously believed. The finding challenges long-standing assumptions about magma and raises an intriguing possibility: oxygen released from Earth's interior may have helped transform the planet's atmosphere billions of years ago.

Through high-pressure experiments and advanced computer simulations, researchers found that magma can absorb additional oxygen beyond the amount normally required by its chemical composition. This hidden oxygen could provide a previously unrecognized connection between Earth's deep interior, volcanic activity, and the development of an oxygen-rich atmosphere.

The research was led by Dr. Yanhao Lin and Dr. Ho-kwang Mao of the Center for High Pressure Science and Technology Advanced Research (HPSTAR), working with Prof. Haiyang Niu of Northwestern Polytechnical University and Prof. Wim van Westrenen of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Their findings were published in National Science Review.

Scientists Challenge a Long-Standing Assumption About Magma

Oxygen is one of the most abundant elements inside Earth, accounting for more than half of the atoms in the planet's silicate interior. Silicates are minerals and molten materials composed primarily of silicon and oxygen, along with other elements. They make up much of Earth's mantle and crust.

Despite oxygen's abundance, scientists have traditionally assumed that magma can contain only a specific amount of it. Under this understanding, the oxygen content is determined by the quantities and electrical charge states of other elements in the molten rock, including silicon, magnesium, and iron.

Water and carbon dioxide behave differently. Both can dissolve in magma and later escape as gases when the surrounding pressure decreases. These substances are known as volatile components, and their release plays an important role in volcanic activity.

Oxygen, however, has generally not been treated as a separate volatile substance that magma can absorb and release. Whether molten silicate rock could hold additional oxygen independently of its ordinary chemical composition remained largely unexplored.

The new research suggests that this assumption may need to change.

Extreme Pressure Reveals Hidden Oxygen in Molten Rock

To investigate, the scientists recreated conditions found deep within Earth using laboratory equipment capable of generating extraordinary pressures and temperatures.

They heated a synthetic version of mid-ocean ridge basalt, a type of volcanic rock commonly produced where tectonic plates move apart beneath the oceans. The samples were exposed to pressures ranging from normal atmospheric pressure to 7 gigapascals and temperatures between 1200 and 1800 °C.

A pressure of 7 gigapascals is approximately 69,000 times the atmospheric pressure at Earth's surface.

The team used specialized piston-cylinder and cubic presses to maintain these extreme conditions. They also added platinum oxide (PtO2) to establish an oxygen-rich environment and test how much additional oxygen the molten rock could absorb.

After the experiments, the researchers rapidly cooled the molten material, producing glass that preserved important characteristics of the melt. They then analyzed its elemental composition and measured the amounts of water and carbon dioxide present.

By calculating how much oxygen was needed to balance the other elements, along with the oxygen already contained in water and carbon dioxide, the scientists could estimate how much remained unaccounted for.

They called this additional amount "excess oxygen."

The results revealed a striking relationship between pressure and oxygen storage.

At normal atmospheric pressure, the glass contained almost no excess oxygen. At 7 gigapascals, however, excess oxygen accounted for more than 5% of the sample's weight.

For comparison, experiments conducted at similar pressures and temperatures without added platinum oxide produced excess oxygen concentrations of only 0.2% to 0.5% by weight.

The researchers also wanted to determine whether the additional oxygen was truly incorporated into the material or merely trapped as tiny gas bubbles.

Using Raman spectroscopy, a technique that identifies substances by examining how they interact with light, they found no detectable signature of oxygen gas in the glass. This indicated that the excess oxygen had become part of the glass structure rather than accumulating in bubbles.

The measured concentrations may even underestimate magma's actual oxygen-storage capacity. Some oxygen could have escaped while the molten samples were cooling, meaning the original melts may have contained still greater amounts.

Computer Simulations Reveal How Magma Stores Extra Oxygen

To better understand the discovery at the atomic level, Prof. Niu led a series of theoretical computer simulations.

The researchers used deep neural network (DNN) models to simulate interactions among atoms with accuracy approaching that of ab initio calculations, which describe atomic behavior using fundamental principles of quantum mechanics.

The simulations showed that additional oxygen could dissolve into molten material until the system reached equilibrium, a state in which oxygen entering and leaving the melt is balanced.

Although the computer models used a simplified system containing only magnesium, silicon, and oxygen, they reproduced the same overall pattern observed in the laboratory: magma's ability to hold excess oxygen increased with pressure.

The simulated oxygen concentrations were lower than the experimental measurements, which the scientists attributed to differences between the simplified model and the more complex chemical composition of actual basalt.

The calculations also revealed changes in how oxygen atoms behaved as more oxygen entered the melt. Their electrical charges became more varied, and a small proportion formed peroxide-like bonds, in which oxygen atoms bond to one another.

These changes help explain how molten rock might accommodate oxygen beyond the amount predicted by conventional chemical models.

Importantly, the pressure-dependent behavior resembles that of water and carbon dioxide, which also become more soluble in magma as pressure increases.

Based on these findings, the researchers propose that oxygen should be recognized as an independent component of silicate melts, rather than being considered only in relation to other elements.

Could Ancient Volcanoes Have Helped Oxygenate Earth's Atmosphere?

The discovery raises a much larger question about Earth's history: Could magma have transported significant amounts of oxygen from the planet's interior to its surface?

The researchers suggest a possible mechanism involving magma generated in oxidized regions of Earth's mantle.

Under the immense pressures deep underground, this magma could absorb substantial quantities of excess oxygen. As it moves upward, the surrounding pressure decreases, reducing the amount of oxygen the molten rock can retain.

Some of that oxygen could then be released, potentially contributing to chemical reactions that increase the oxidation of the upper mantle, Earth's crust, and eventually the atmosphere.

Oxidation refers to chemical processes involving the transfer of electrons. In this context, oxygen carried by magma could increase the oxidizing capacity of surrounding materials and potentially influence the balance of oxygen in the atmosphere.

This proposed mechanism may also help explain an intriguing coincidence in Earth's geological past.

Between approximately 2.5 billion and 2.0 billion years ago, atmospheric oxygen levels underwent major increases. This interval overlaps with the formation of some of Earth's largest large igneous provinces (LIPs), enormous regions of volcanic rock created by exceptionally large outpourings of magma.

The researchers suggest that oxygen released from these ancient volcanic systems could have contributed to changes in atmospheric composition.

Their preliminary calculation highlights the potentially enormous scale of the process. They estimate that if magma erupted during this period released excess oxygen equal to just 0.27% of its weight, the total amount could theoretically match all the oxygen present in Earth's atmosphere today.

This does not establish that volcanic activity actually supplied that much atmospheric oxygen. Instead, it illustrates how even a relatively small release of oxygen from immense quantities of magma could have major planetary consequences.

A New Clue to Earth's Evolution and Habitable Planets

The findings could influence several important areas of planetary science.

For one, they may change how scientists understand ancient magma oceans, vast regions of molten rock believed to have existed during the early evolution of Earth and other rocky planets.

They also introduce a possible new factor in volcanic degassing, the process through which gases and other volatile substances escape from molten rock and interact with a planet's atmosphere.

If magma can store and release oxygen independently of its other chemical components, models of Earth's atmospheric development may need to account for this previously overlooked process.

The implications could extend beyond Earth. Understanding how oxygen moves between the interiors and atmospheres of rocky planets may help researchers investigate the conditions that allow potentially habitable environments to develop and persist over billions of years.

Although further research is needed to establish how much oxygen natural magmas carry and how much reaches the atmosphere, the discovery points to a surprising possibility: some of the processes that helped shape Earth's oxygen-rich environment may have originated far beneath the planet's surface.

#741. Scientists discover a secret glow in toxic fire salamanders

Fire salamanders are among Europe's most recognizable amphibians, known for their striking black and yellow coloring and the poisonous substances they release to deter predators. Despite their familiar appearance, scientists are still uncovering surprising details about their biology. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classifies the species as "vulnerable" on its Red List of Threatened Species. Fire salamanders typically inhabit damp forests, streams, and mountainous regions, where habitat destruction and fragmentation increasingly threaten their survival.

New research has revealed that fire salamanders possess an unexpected ability to fluoresce under ultraviolet light. The glow is most pronounced on the yellow underside of their bodies and along their sides. Researchers traced the fluorescence primarily to glands in the animals' skin and the substances those glands release. Remarkably, these secretions can remain fluorescent for more than 24 hours after leaving the salamander's body.

"It is fascinating that such a well-studied species still harbors unknown phenomena like this. It reminds us that even the most familiar organisms can hide secrets that are only revealed when they are observed with new tools," says Bernat Burriel, a researcher at the Museum of Natural Sciences in Barcelona and the study's first author.

The phenomenon occurs when compounds in the salamander's skin absorb ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see, and reemit that energy as visible light. This process produces vivid green and cyan colors. Known as biofluorescence, it requires an outside source of illumination and should not be confused with bioluminescence. Animals such as fireflies produce their own light through chemical reactions, while fluorescent organisms must first absorb light from their surroundings.

Scientists once believed that biofluorescence occurred almost exclusively in marine organisms, with scorpions standing out as an unusual example on land. More recent studies have challenged that assumption, identifying fluorescent properties in a growing variety of terrestrial animals, including reptiles, birds, and amphibians.

Although researchers have confirmed that fire salamanders fluoresce, the biological purpose of this ability remains uncertain. One possibility is that the glow serves as a form of communication, helping individuals recognize one another or assess potential mates. Another is that it makes their warning coloration more noticeable to predators.

"Fluorescence meets several criteria that suggest a communicative function. It could help salamanders detect each other in nocturnal or particularly dense environments, or act as an additional defense signal," says Martin Kaltenpoth, director of the Department of Insect Symbiosis at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology and a co-author of the study.

The discovery that toxic skin secretions are also fluorescent raises additional questions about how salamanders interact with predators and other animals in their environment.

For now, these proposed functions remain hypotheses. Animals with particularly sensitive vision may be able to detect the green and cyan fluorescence even when it is extremely faint. Humans, however, need a UV lamp to observe the effect.

In the forests where fire salamanders live, nighttime illumination comes primarily from moonlight and starlight. Researchers note that full moonlight contains a greater proportion of ultraviolet and violet wavelengths than daylight, which has a more evenly distributed spectrum. Under these conditions, fluorescence could create small green and cyan highlights against the salamanders' yellow markings, potentially making them easier for other salamanders to spot.

Could the Fluorescent Glow Warn Predators?

Another possible explanation involves aposematism, a defensive strategy in which animals display conspicuous colors to advertise that they are poisonous or otherwise dangerous. Fire salamanders already use their distinctive yellow and black patterns as warning signals, and fluorescence might provide an additional visual cue.

Scientists established a connection between salamander warning colors and chemical defenses more than a century ago when they identified samandarines. These highly toxic steroidal alkaloids are produced from cholesterol precursors and contribute to the animals' chemical protection.

Despite decades of research into salamander toxins and skin chemistry, the newly observed fluorescence came as a surprise.

"The presence of this fluorescent compound was surprising because salamander skin secretions have been studied chemically for decades, and we were unaware of any published reports on fluorescence," says Andrés Brunetti, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology and a co-first author of the study.

One of the biggest unanswered questions concerns the substance responsible for the fluorescence. Researchers have not yet determined its chemical identity, although the evidence suggests it may be a molecule not previously recognized in fire salamanders.

"We still don't know what the compound responsible for this fluorescence is, but everything indicates that it is a molecule unknown until now in this species. Identifying it will be key to understanding its origin and function," adds Salvador Carranza, a researcher at the IBE (CSIC-UPF) and another co-author of the study.

The team is now working to identify and chemically characterize potential compounds responsible for the effect. Determining which molecule produces the glow could help explain how the fluorescence develops and whether it plays a meaningful role in salamander behavior or survival.

A New Discovery With Implications for Amphibian Conservation

Beyond revealing an unexpected feature of a familiar species, the findings demonstrate how new research techniques can uncover biological traits that have escaped scientific attention for decades.

Understanding whether fluorescence influences communication, mating, or predator avoidance could also contribute to conservation efforts. Such information may help researchers better understand the behavior and ecological needs of fire salamanders, which already face significant threats from habitat loss and fragmentation.

The research also involved scientists from the Institute of Subtropical Biology and the Catalan Society of Herpetology. It forms part of a pioneering amphibian conservation project in Catalonia supported by the Barcelona Zoo Foundation.
